title: Why It's Called 'Open Source': a 1998 Naming Decision
explainer: The phrase 'open source' is not as old as the practice it describes - it was proposed by Christine Peterson at a February 1998 strategy meeting in Palo Alto, called right after Netscape announced it would release its browser's source code. The group deliberately chose a less political label than 'free software' to make the approach easier to pitch to businesses, and Bruce Perens and Eric Raymond founded the Open Source Initiative weeks later to define and steward it. Large-scale, cross-company contribution depends on that branding choice having separated the practice from any single ideology.

title: Stallman's 1989 GPL and the Legal Machinery Behind Shared Code
explainer: Contributing to open source at scale depends on licensing, and the modern template for that is Richard Stallman's GNU General Public License, first published in 1989 after he generalized similar one-off licenses he had written for GNU Emacs, GDB, and GCC. Its 'copyleft' mechanism - requiring derivative works to stay under the same license - is what lets thousands of unrelated contributors build on a shared codebase without a single contribution quietly becoming someone's private, closed fork. That history is why license choice, not just code review, is part of contributing at scale.
